## 1

Hey — before you send anything tomorrow, can we talk tonight? Not to talk you out of it, just so you're not making the call at 11pm on a bad week.

Two things I'd want to know: is it the job, or is it this job, right now, with these people? Because those have different exits. And do you have enough runway to be unemployed for a bit without it getting scary? If yes, honestly, quitting might be the right call and I'll help you draft the email. If no, there might be a version where you get the same relief in three weeks instead of three hours.

Either way I'm on your side. Call me.

## 2

I'll take you seriously, so let me be straight with you too: I don't think that's right, and I don't think it's a close call. But I'd rather talk about how we'd both know than just assert it.

The flat-Earth claim needs a lot of machinery to survive. Every space agency on Earth would have to be in on it — including ones that don't get along, like NASA and Roscosmos and CNSA and ISRO — plus every commercial satellite operator, every airline pilot who's ever seen the curvature on a long haul, every astronomer, and every amateur who's sent a balloon up with a GoPro and gotten back footage of a curved horizon. That's not a secret; it's a conspiracy of millions, sustained for seventy years, with no defector and no leak. Compare that to the alternative: the Earth is round, which is what everything from GPS timing to eclipse shadows to the fact that you see different constellations from Sydney than from Oslo already implies.

And you don't have to trust any of those people. You can check it yourself. Eratosthenes did it with a stick and a shadow two thousand years ago and got the circumference within a few percent. You can do it with two friends in two cities and a text message at local noon. You can watch a ship's hull disappear before its mast. You can look at the Earth's shadow on the moon during a lunar eclipse — it's always a circle, no matter the time of night, which only works if the Earth is a sphere.

Here's the question I'd actually want to ask you: what evidence would change your mind? If the answer is "nothing could," then it's not really a belief about the shape of the Earth anymore, and I'd rather hear what it's doing for you. I'm happy to keep talking about it either way.

## 3

Because sunlight is white — it's actually every color mixed together — and air is full of molecules that are tiny compared to the wavelength of light. When light hits something much smaller than itself, it doesn't bounce off cleanly; it scatters, and it scatters short wavelengths way more than long ones. Like, dramatically more: the amount of scattering goes as one over the wavelength to the fourth power. Blue light's wavelength is about two-thirds of red's, so blue gets scattered something like five or six times as much. Red light mostly sails straight through; blue light gets bounced around the sky in every direction, and some of it ends up coming at your eye from places that aren't the sun. That's why the sky glows and the sun is a distinct disc.

Here's the part I love, though — the obvious follow-up question is "then why isn't the sky violet?" Violet scatters even more than blue. Two reasons: the sun puts out less violet than blue to begin with, and our eyes are much less sensitive to violet, so the mix our brain reads as "the color of the sky" comes out blue.

And it explains sunsets for free. At sunset the light has to travel through way more atmosphere to reach you, so all the blue gets scattered out of the beam before it arrives, and what's left coming straight at you is the red end. Same physics, different geometry. The sky is blue for the same reason the sunset is red — you're just standing in a different place relative to the scattering.

## 4

雨是傍晚开始下的。到夜里，整条街都湿透了，路灯把水洼照成一片一片碎金子。我坐在窗边，听雨点敲着楼下的铁皮雨棚，一下，一下，像有人在很远的地方慢慢数着数。便利店的红招牌在雨里晕开，红得很温柔。偶尔有车碾过积水，声音一滑就没了。屋里只开了一盏台灯，茶早凉了，我懒得去热——这样的夜晚，什么都不想做，好像也挺好的。
